title: Workspace convergence of the rand 0.9 ecosystem
description:
`rand_chacha` and `rand_core` 0.9 are declared once in `[workspace.dependencies]`, with `gf2-sim` — the one workspace member consuming them today — inheriting that declaration, so the campaign's random-number source has one version the workspace agrees on.

## Background

A published sampling dataset must let any shard be regenerated from its address alone, so the random-matrix source has to be version-stable; a version that drifts per crate is how a dataset silently stops being regenerable. Three `rand_chacha` majors and two `rand` majors coexist today: the workspace declares `rand = "0.8"` and no `rand_chacha` at all (`Cargo.toml:27`); `gf2-sim` pins `rand_chacha = "0.9"` with `rand = "0.9"` directly (`crates/gf2-sim/Cargo.toml:18-19`); `gf2-kernels-hip` pins the same pair as development dependencies (`crates/gf2-kernels-hip/Cargo.toml:33-34`); `gf2-coding` pins an optional `rand_chacha = "0.3"` (`crates/gf2-coding/Cargo.toml:23`), which belongs to the `rand` 0.8 ecosystem; and `gf2-core` uses the workspace `rand = "0.8"`. `@/inv/convention-convergence` requires a shared convention to have one form; this change is where that convergence happens for the 0.9 ecosystem.

One constraint shapes how far the convergence reaches: `gf2-kernels-hip` is excluded from the workspace (`Cargo.toml`, `exclude`) because it needs ROCm to build, so it has no workspace parent to inherit from and cannot use `workspace = true`; it follows the same versions by explicit pin.

The `gf2-coding` holdout is recorded as a named exception by its own documentation leaf behind this one; nothing in this change migrates the 0.8 ecosystem.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: `rand_chacha` and `rand_core` are declared once in `[workspace.dependencies]` at version 0.9, and `gf2-sim` — the one workspace member consuming them today — consumes them through `workspace = true`, its direct pins replaced in this change.
- [hard] REQ-02: `gf2-kernels-hip`, which the workspace excludes because it requires ROCm to build and which therefore cannot inherit workspace dependencies, pins the same 0.9 versions explicitly, with a comment naming the exclusion as the reason it cannot inherit.
- [hard] REQ-03: The workspace builds and its tests pass with no crate resolving two `rand_chacha` 0.9 copies, verifiable from the lockfile.

## Notes

Scope is the version migration alone: no new crate, no sampler code, and no exception documentation land here.

planning.outcome: rand_chacha/rand_core 0.9 declared once at workspace level, with gf2-sim inheriting and gf2-kernels-hip pinned to match

terminal.consumer_family: workspace crates consuming the rand 0.9 ecosystem
terminal.test_boundary: workspace cargo-ci build with lockfile duplicate check
terminal.worker_sized_reason: One workspace-dependency promotion across three manifests is a small self-contained cycle.

title: Named exception record for the rand 0.8 holdout
description:
`gf2-coding`'s optional `rand_chacha = "0.3"` is recorded as a named exception to the workspace's converged `rand` 0.9 ecosystem, with a tracked convergence condition, so the divergence is a cited decision rather than an unremarked drift.

## Background

`@/inv/convention-convergence` treats a parallel variant of a shared convention as a defect unless it is a named, cited exception with a tracked convergence condition. After the workspace converges on `rand_chacha` 0.9, `gf2-coding`'s optional `rand_chacha = "0.3"` (`crates/gf2-coding/Cargo.toml:23`) is exactly such a variant: it belongs to the `rand` 0.8 ecosystem the crate still builds against, and migrating it is out of scope for this campaign.

The repository tracks such exceptions in place rather than in a central registry, so the record lands beside the two declarations it concerns: the workspace `[workspace.dependencies]` block and the `gf2-coding` pin itself.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A comment beside the `[workspace.dependencies]` `rand_chacha` declaration names `gf2-coding`'s optional `rand_chacha = "0.3"` as the one exception, states that it belongs to the `rand` 0.8 ecosystem, and states the tracked convergence condition that it migrates when `gf2-coding` moves to `rand` 0.9.
- [hard] REQ-02: A comment beside the `gf2-coding` pin cites `@/inv/convention-convergence` and points at the workspace declaration as the converged form.
- [hard] REQ-03: The workspace builds unchanged; the change is documentation only.

## Notes

Scope is the exception record alone; no dependency version changes here.

title: Empty gf2-stats workspace member crate
description:
The new narrow statistics crate exists as an empty workspace member with its identity stated, ready to receive the sampler and the estimators in their own leaves.

## Background

The campaign's sampler and statistics live in a new narrow workspace crate rather than in `gf2-core`, where interval estimators have no home, or `gf2-algebra`, where a statistics layer strains the crate's stated identity. The crate depends only on `gf2-core` among workspace crates, which keeps `@/inv/crate-dependency-direction` trivially satisfied and keeps the sampler usable from validation harnesses that never touch a permanent kernel.

The foundation is its own leaf so that the crate's placement, metadata, and identity are reviewable once, and every later statistics leaf registers one module against a crate that already builds.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A workspace member crate `gf2-stats` builds with `gf2-core` as its only in-workspace dependency.
- [hard] REQ-02: The crate consumes `rand_chacha` and `rand_core` through `workspace = true`, inheriting the converged 0.9 declarations.
- [hard] REQ-03: The crate README states the crate's identity as the narrow statistics layer and names the sampler, interval estimators, exact tests, and accumulator as the surfaces that will live in it.
- [hard] REQ-04: `cargo test -p gf2-stats` passes on the empty crate, so the member wiring is demonstrated before any module lands.

## Notes

Scope is the crate skeleton alone. No sampler, estimator, or test-vector code lands here.

title: Uniform $\mathbb{F}_q$ matrix sampler with domain-separated streams
description: A production sampler that draws uniform random matrices over $\mathbb{F}_q$ for $q \in \{3,5,7\}$ from a reproducible address space whose purposes and streams are injective by construction, hosted in a new narrow workspace crate. ## Background A published sampling dataset must let any shard be regenerated from its address alone, so the random-matrix source has to be version-stable and partitioned by construction rather than by audit. Two in-tree generators fall short of that. `gf2_algebra::testutil::random_matrix` reduces an MMIX LCG output modulo $q$ and is a test helper. `FieldMatrix::random_seeded` (`crates/gf2-core/src/field/matrix.rs:617`) takes a single `u64` seed, draws through `StdRng` — whose algorithm carries no cross-version reproducibility guarantee, so a dataset seeded through it stops being regenerable after a dependency bump — offers no partition of the stream space, and produces `FieldMatrix>`. The gap is therefore not the absence of a uniform sampler but the absence of one with domain-separated, reproducible stream addressing. Rejection sampling is required rather than optional. The sampler consumes bytes and $256 \bmod 7 = 4$, so reducing a byte without rejection would give four residues probability $37/256$ and three of them $36/256$ against a uniform $1/7$. In relative terms the worst class is off by $1.56\%$, about $22$ times the $0.07\%$ relative resolution a standard error of $10^{-4}$ on $\Pr[\mathrm{per}(A)=0] \approx 1/7$ represents. A prototype carrying these properties, with entry-uniformity and stream-separation tests, is `dev/research/permanent-sampling-feas/src/sampler.rs`; it is the reference to lift from. The ground this module stands on is laid by prerequisite leaves: `rand_chacha` and `rand_core` 0.9 are declared once at workspace level, and the `gf2-stats` member crate exists with `gf2-core` as its only in-workspace dependency. This leaf registers the sampler module in that crate and implements it. ## Success Criteria - [hard] REQ-01: Matrix draws use ChaCha20 seeded from a 32-byte block of four little-endian `u64` words: campaign root, $q$, $n$, and a fourth word whose top $8$ bits hold the purpose tag and whose low $56$ bits hold the stream index. - [hard] REQ-02: Seed derivation asserts the stream index is below $2^{56}$ and refuses to derive otherwise, so the map from $(\text{root}, q, n, \text{purpose}, \text{stream})$ to seed block is injective by construction rather than by convention. - [hard] REQ-03: Entries are exactly uniform over $\mathbb{F}_q$: a test draws at least $3 \times 10^5$ entries per field for $q \in \{3,5,7\}$ and finds each residue class within six binomial standard errors of $1/q$. - [hard] REQ-04: Address separation is asserted at the address level: a test over a set of addresses differing in each component in turn finds every derived seed block distinct, and a further test finds two generators started from distinct addresses diverge in their raw output stream. - [hard] REQ-05: Committed golden vectors pin, for a fixed set of addresses spanning each field and each purpose tag, the derived 32-byte seed block and the first drawn matrix, and a test compares against them. - [hard] REQ-06: Two draws from one address tuple return identical matrices, demonstrated by test. - [hard] REQ-07: The draw-to-entry mapping is documented and tested as $A[k / n][k \bmod n]$ row-major for draw index $k$, before any packed constructor reorders it into kernel storage. - [hard] REQ-08: A draw fills a caller-supplied row-major entry buffer without a per-draw heap allocation, so a caller can pack directly into the permanent kernels' matrix types. ## Notes Stream separation is a statement about addresses and generator state, not about output values: two disjoint streams may legitimately draw the same small matrix, and at $q = 3$, $n = 2$ there are only $81$ matrices in total. Tests therefore assert distinct derived seeds, distinct generator output, and golden-vector agreement, never that two streams share no matrix. The crate carries no dependency on the algebra layer: packing into kernel matrix types is the caller's concern, which keeps the sampler usable from validation harnesses that never touch a permanent kernel.

planning.outcome: Production ChaCha20 rejection sampler in gf2-stats, addressing matrices by campaign root, field, size, purpose and stream

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One module lifted from a tested prototype plus its golden-vector tests fits one focused cycle.

title: Wilson score interval estimator
description:
The campaign's working confidence interval: a Wilson score interval over a count out of $N$, validated against an independent computation of its own definition and well-formed at the campaign's largest sample size.

## Background

Every published Monte Carlo estimate in this repository states its sample count and an interval. The only interval implemented in-tree today is a Wilson score interval in a research prototype (`dev/research/permanent-sampling-feas/src/stats.rs:38`); the production statistics crate has none. Wilson is the campaign's working interval at large counts, where it is accurate and short; the conservative small-count estimator is separate work behind this leaf on a dependency edge, in the same module.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A Wilson score interval is returned for a count out of $N$ at a caller-supplied level, agreeing to within $10^{-12}$ with an independently computed reference on hand-checked cases including $Z = 0$ and $Z = N$.
- [hard] REQ-02: The estimator returns a well-formed interval at the campaign's largest planned sample size, $N = 2 \times 10^{7}$, with no overflow, no interval of negative width, and no bound outside $[0,1]$.
- [hard] REQ-03: The entry point takes counts, not samples, so it is usable both online against a running accumulator and offline against a published dataset.

## Notes

Scope is the Wilson estimator alone; the Clopper-Pearson estimator, the coverage demonstration, and the which-regime documentation follow in the dependent leaf.

title: Clopper-Pearson interval estimator with coverage demonstration
description:
The conservative small-count interval: a Clopper-Pearson estimator validated against an independent inversion of its own definition, with empirical coverage demonstrated in the regime the rectangular validation lives in.

## Background

No Clopper-Pearson estimator exists anywhere in-tree, and the rectangular validation cells — where the estimated event probability is of order $q^{-n}$ and counts are in the tens — are exactly where a normal-approximation interval's coverage is weakest. Clopper-Pearson is conservative by construction and keeps its nominal coverage at counts in the tens.

The two estimators answer different questions. Checking one against the other proves nothing — containment follows from how they are built — so this estimator is validated against an independent computation of its own definition, and its coverage is demonstrated empirically rather than assumed from construction.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A Clopper-Pearson interval is returned for a count out of $N$ at a caller-supplied level and matches, to a stated tolerance, an independent computation of its own bounds by inversion of the binomial tail or equivalently by beta quantiles, on cases spanning $Z = 0$, $Z = N$, and counts in the tens.
- [hard] REQ-02: Coverage is demonstrated empirically: over repeated simulated draws at stated $(N, p)$ including small $N$ and small $p$, the fraction of intervals containing $p$ is at least the nominal level.
- [hard] REQ-03: The estimator returns a well-formed interval at $N = 2 \times 10^{7}$, with no overflow, no interval of negative width, and no bound outside $[0,1]$.
- [hard] REQ-04: Documentation states which estimator suits which regime, so a caller at counts in the tens is not left with the normal-approximation interval by default.

## Notes

Entry points take counts, not samples, matching the Wilson estimator beside it, so both are usable online against a running accumulator and offline against a published dataset.

planning.outcome: A Clopper-Pearson estimator checked by independent inversion, with empirical coverage demonstrated at small counts

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One estimator function with its inversion check and coverage demonstration fits one focused cycle.

title: Preregistered exact binomial tests for campaign cells
description:
The two exact binomial tests the campaign's acceptance decisions rest on, with a result interface that stays correct where an exact tail underflows double precision.

## Background

The campaign's acceptance decisions rest on two nulls known exactly rather than approximately. The permanent floor $\Pr[\mathrm{per}(A) = 0] \ge 1/q$ is a composite null whose worst case is $p = 1/q$, so a test evaluated there is valid against the whole null. The determinant companion is pinned at the exact finite-$n$ value $1 - \prod_{i=1}^{n}(1 - q^{-i})$. Both are binomial observations of a count out of a fixed $N$, so both admit an exact $p$-value; the normal-approximation critical values that appear in planning arithmetic ($z = 3.16$ one-sided, $z = 3.36$ two-sided at a family of $63$ cells) are sizing tools, not decision rules.

Exactness has a numerical consequence the interface must face rather than hide. At $N = 2 \times 10^{7}$ a preregistered per-cell level of order $10^{-4}$ sits far out in the distribution, and the exact tail sum legitimately underflows double precision. An interface returning a plain probability silently reports zero there, which is indistinguishable from a catastrophic disagreement and equally indistinguishable from a bug.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A one-sided exact binomial test of the composite null $\Pr[\mathrm{per}(A) = 0] \ge 1/q$ evaluates the null at its worst case $p = 1/q$ and returns a result from the binomial distribution, matching a brute-force sum over the probability mass function for $N \le 200$.
- [hard] REQ-02: A two-sided exact binomial test against a caller-supplied exact probability returns a result under a stated and documented two-sided convention, matching a brute-force sum for $N \le 200$.
- [hard] REQ-03: The result interface reports on a log scale, or as a direct comparison against a caller-supplied threshold, so a decision stays correct where the exact tail underflows double precision.
- [hard] REQ-04: A test at $N = 2 \times 10^{7}$ with a preregistered per-cell level returns a decision and a finite log-scale statistic rather than a probability that has flushed to zero, for counts on both sides of the threshold.
- [hard] REQ-05: A level-allocation helper divides a caller-supplied error budget across a caller-supplied number of tests and returns the per-test level, documented so one global budget can be split across more than one test family.
- [hard] REQ-06: Documentation states that normal-approximation critical values are planning approximations for sizing, and that acceptance decisions use these exact tests.

## Notes

The tests take counts and a null value, so the same entry points serve a running campaign and a later reanalysis of a published dataset.

planning.outcome: Exact one-sided floor test and two-sided determinant test with a result interface that stays correct where tails underflow

terminal.worker_sized_reason: Two exact tests with one result interface fits one focused cycle.

title: Checkpointable streaming shard accumulator
description:
A streaming accumulator that pools per-shard permanent and determinant zero counts with atomic commits, duplicate rejection, order-independent pooling, and exact replay after interruption.

## Background

A campaign cell runs for hours and is assembled from many independently addressed shards, produced in arbitrary order and possibly concurrently. Pooling those shards is where a sampling campaign silently corrupts itself: a shard counted twice shrinks the interval around a wrong estimate, and a shard lost to an interrupted write leaves an estimate whose sample count does not match its data. Both failure modes have already occurred in this problem family — a superseded measurement round pooled overlapping streams and reported an apparent below-floor signal that independent re-measurement dissolved.

Existing in-tree statistics code has no accumulator type and no serialisation: the prototype's row type derives only `Clone` and `Debug` and leaves the crate as a formatted CSV line. Restart behaviour is therefore new work rather than a lift.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A shard's counts enter the pooled state exactly once and as a unit; an interrupted commit leaves the pooled state as if that shard had never been offered, demonstrated by a test that interrupts mid-commit.
- [hard] REQ-02: Offering a shard whose identity is already committed is rejected and reported to the caller, never silently merged and never double-counted.
- [hard] REQ-03: Pooling one set of shards yields byte-identical pooled state under any offer order, demonstrated over a shuffled permutation set in a test.
- [hard] REQ-04: Restoring from a serialised snapshot and continuing reproduces the counts of an uninterrupted run over the same shard set, bit for bit.
- [hard] REQ-05: Pooled state carries, per cell, the matrix count, the permanent zero count, and the histogram of permanent values over the $q$ residue classes.
- [hard] REQ-06: Pooled state carries the determinant companion as a sample count with a zero count, or as an explicit not-evaluated state, so a cell that ran without the companion is distinguishable from one that evaluated $N$ matrices and found none singular.
- [hard] REQ-07: A shard whose production or evaluation failed is retained with its identity and failure reason, excluded from the pooled state until explicitly readmitted, and visible to the caller in that quarantined state.
- [hard] REQ-08: The accumulator state serialises to a self-describing snapshot carrying a schema version, and a snapshot whose schema version differs from the reader's is refused rather than misread.
- [hard] REQ-09: Pooled state carries the per-shard identities that produced it, so the sample count behind an estimate is derivable from the state alone.

## Notes

The snapshot type is plain serialisable data with no dependency on any checkpoint-file mechanism, so persistence policy stays with the orchestration layer that owns crash-safe writing.

planning.outcome: Streaming accumulator whose shard commits are atomic, duplicate-rejecting, order-independent when pooled, and exactly replayable after interruption

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One accumulator type with its snapshot contract fits one focused cycle.

title: Generic checkpoint payload mechanism
description:
The crash-safe checkpoint writer and reader in the simulation crate become generic over a serialisable payload and a configuration-hash provider, so a second campaign reuses the mechanism instead of copying it.

## Background

`crates/gf2-sim/src/checkpoint/mod.rs` implements a mature and tested crash-safe checkpoint mechanism: a PID-tagged temporary file, fsync, rename, and directory fsync, guarded by a blake3 hash over the serialised configuration so a resume against a different configuration is a hard error, with a reader that rejects a wrong schema version or a hash mismatch rather than silently accepting it. Its behaviour is pinned by a resume-versus-uninterrupted counter-equality test and a signal-and-resume byte-identity subprocess test.

What is not reusable is the schema: the payload type is fixed to a fielded record of coding-domain quantities, and the writer is typed to that record rather than to a payload. A second campaign with different axes therefore cannot use the writer as it stands. The repository's convention rule holds that a shared mechanism has one form and that a private helper duplicating a shared mechanism is a defect unless it is a named, tracked exception; "write a checkpoint crash-safely and refuse to resume against a different configuration" is that shared mechanism, whatever the payload. Changing it at its source is the resolution taken here.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The checkpoint writer and reader are generic over a serialisable payload type and a configuration-hash provider, with the previously hard-coded payload becoming one instantiation.
- [hard] REQ-02: The atomic write path is behaviourally unchanged: PID-tagged temporary file, fsync, rename, directory fsync, and crash safety under a signal delivered during the write.
- [hard] REQ-03: A reader refuses a checkpoint whose schema version, payload identity, or configuration hash disagrees with the caller's, and treats an absent file as fresh work.
- [hard] REQ-04: A second, unrelated payload type round-trips through the same writer and reader in a test, demonstrating the mechanism has one form.
- [hard] REQ-05: Module documentation describes the payload contract a new caller must satisfy, and no documentation still describes the writer as specific to one campaign's record.

## Notes

Scope is the generic mechanism alone, demonstrated by a fresh payload round-trip. Migrating the existing simulation pipeline onto the generic form, with its regression tests, is separate work behind this leaf on a dependency edge.

Deterministic resume in the existing implementation works by storing each worker's absolute generator word position; the generic payload contract must leave that pattern expressible rather than assume a particular resume key.

planning.outcome: Simulation checkpoint writer and reader carry any serialisable payload behind a config-hash provider, with resume behaviour unchanged

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One genericisation of an existing tested module, demonstrated by a fresh payload round-trip, fits one focused cycle.

title: Versioned dataset layout and record schemas
description:
The published shape of a permanent zero-fraction dataset: a versioned campaign home, the root manifest schema, the per-shard and per-summary record schemas, the writer-role partition, and the documentation that lets a reader navigate it.

## Background

No manifest convention exists anywhere in this repository: a search for manifest files under the documentation tree returns nothing. The closest precedent, a per-curve README generated by an existing campaign binary, records invocation, configuration, host and wall-clock but records no git revision and no toolchain version. The repository requires every published number to trace to a committed artefact recording seeds, git revision, hardware and toolchain, so this schema is new work rather than an adaptation.

The dataset home is `dev/simulation_results/permanent-zero-fraction/<campaign-id>/`. This is a deliberate divergence from the earlier design sketch, which proposed `dev/campaigns/`: both directories are declared permanent documentation areas, but the development index classifies `dev/campaigns` as simulation campaign *definitions* and `dev/simulation_results` as campaign *outputs*, and today `dev/campaigns` holds only campaign configuration files. A published dataset is an output.

Two structural rules travel with the layout. Each file in the raw set has exactly one writer role, so a field's execution owns its own paths and campaign-scoped paths belong to finalization; concurrent field executions then never write one file. And the tree is partitioned into raw data and derived artefacts, because an integrity file covering documents that quote it could never be closed.

An earlier review cycle in this problem family recorded the cost of mixing interpretation into generated output: receipts carrying interpretive prose had to be regenerated every time a claim's wording changed, which was its largest single source of rework. The schema therefore admits data and mechanical provenance fields only.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A dataset lives at `dev/simulation_results/permanent-zero-fraction/<campaign-id>/` and contains a root manifest, per-shard records under `shards/q<q>/n<nn>/`, one summary per field under `summaries/`, a pooled `summary.csv`, and an integrity file.
- [hard] REQ-02: The root manifest schema carries the campaign root seed; the stream purpose namespace with each purpose's tag; the cell grid with per-cell $N$, shard size and shard identities; the backend selected per cell; whether the determinant companion runs at each cell; the git revision; the compiler and accelerator runtime versions; the CPU and GPU models; and a schema version.
- [hard] REQ-03: A per-shard record schema carries the stream address, matrix count, permanent zero count, and the histogram of permanent values over the $q$ residue classes.
- [hard] REQ-04: A record and a summary row express the determinant companion as a sample count with a zero count, or as an explicit not-evaluated state; a cell that ran without the companion never stores a numeric zero count, which would be indistinguishable from a cell that evaluated its matrices and found none singular.
- [hard] REQ-05: A summary row schema carries, per $(q,n)$, the pooled matrix count, permanent zero count, the determinant fields of REQ-04, and one typed terminal state. A completed state carries point estimates with intervals and acceptance verdicts; a halted state carries only its canonical reason and no final estimates or verdicts.
- [hard] REQ-06: The schema partitions the tree into raw data — manifest, shard records, field summaries, pooled summary — and derived artefacts, and names which is which.
- [hard] REQ-07: The schema assigns each file in the raw set exactly one writer role, with field-scoped paths written by that field's execution and campaign-scoped paths written only by finalization.
- [hard] REQ-08: A schema-conformance check accepts a well-formed dataset and rejects one with a missing required field, an unknown field, or a wrong schema version, exercised in both directions by test.
- [hard] REQ-09: No schema field admits an interpretive statement about what the numbers mean, asserted by a test over the schema's own field list.
- [hard] REQ-10: The layout, the manifest schema, the record schemas, the writer-role partition, the raw-versus-derived boundary, and the rule that a campaign id is never overwritten in place are documented at the dataset home.

## Notes

Storage stays $O(\text{shards})$ because matrices are regenerable from their stream address; a whole cell costs tens of kilobytes.

planning.outcome: Versioned dataset home with a root manifest schema, record schemas, a writer-role partition and a raw-versus-derived boundary

title: Source identity and integrity for published datasets
description:
The rules that make a published dataset traceable to the source that produced it and verifiable by a reader: a build-state guard on the emitting binary, a source-identity rule that survives a dataset living inside the repository, and an integrity file over the raw data with a manifest hash that is not self-referential.

## Background

A self-hash recorded by a binary with no build-state guard proves nothing about the source that produced the numbers: it says only that the binary hashed itself. An earlier review cycle in this problem family recorded that specific defect. So the emitting binary embeds the revision it was built from and checks it before writing.

That check has to be stated carefully, because the dataset lives inside the repository. A rule demanding a wholly clean working tree would deadlock immediately: the first shard written dirties the tree, so the second emission would refuse. What the rule protects is the identity of the *source* behind the numbers, not the absence of output.

The manifest hash needs the same care. A hash stored inside the structure it covers cannot be recomputed by a reader, because recomputing it requires knowing it. Omitting the hash field from the canonical serialisation, or keeping the hash in a sidecar, makes verification a mechanical operation rather than a claim.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The emitting binary embeds the source revision it was built from, and emits only when that embedded revision equals the current `HEAD`.
- [hard] REQ-02: Emission additionally requires that no tracked file differs outside the active campaign's output subtree. Expected raw and derived files under the frozen campaign id are permitted, while a changed source file, a changed build or dependency manifest, a changed protocol document, or a changed root manifest refuses the emission and names what changed.
- [hard] REQ-03: A test drives the rule through both outcomes: a tree dirtied only by the campaign's own outputs under its campaign id emits, and a tree with a modified source file, dependency manifest, or protocol document refuses.
- [hard] REQ-04: The root manifest's content hash is computed over a canonical serialisation from which the hash field itself is omitted, or is held in a sidecar file, and a test confirms a reader recomputes the recorded value from the manifest alone.
- [hard] REQ-05: `checksums.sha256` covers exactly the raw data set and no derived artefact, and its format is documented well enough to verify with standard tooling outside this repository.
- [hard] REQ-06: A verification path re-checks a dataset against its integrity file and reports pass, or the failing paths, distinguishing a missing file from a changed one.
- [hard] REQ-07: A dataset whose recorded git revision names a commit absent from the repository is reported as unverifiable rather than passing silently.

## Notes

title: Checkpointed resume, determinism, and quarantine for the campaign driver

The campaign driver survives interruption: it checkpoints its progress through the generic checkpoint mechanism, resumes to results identical to an uninterrupted run, refuses a changed configuration, and quarantines a failing work item instead of losing it.

title: Determinant companion evaluated on the campaign's matrices
description:
The finite-field determinant is evaluated inside the campaign's composite loop on the same drawn matrices as the permanent, producing per-shard and per-cell determinant counts alongside the permanent ones.

## Background

The determinant companion supplies a pipeline validation the permanent cannot. The count of invertible $n \times n$ matrices over $\mathbb{F}_q$ is $\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}(q^n - q^k)$, so the singular probability is known exactly at every finite size:

$$
\Pr[\det(A) = 0] \;=\; 1 - \prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(1 - q^{-i}\right),
$$

which pins a value at every size the campaign measures, unlike the permanent, whose exact value is available only at the smallest sizes. A determinant curve that misses its own exact values falsifies the pipeline before any permanent conclusion is drawn.

That check only has force if the determinant is computed on the *same* matrices as the permanent. Evaluating it on an independently drawn sample would test a different pipeline than the one producing the published permanent counts, and would leave the shared draw, pack and address path — where this problem family's recorded defects actually occurred — unchecked.

The routine exists and sits below the algebra layer: `FieldMatrix::det` (`crates/gf2-core/src/field/inverse.rs:494`) is a Dumas–Pernet elimination with an explicit permutation sign, generic over the finite-field trait, returning field zero at rank below $n$, so no reverse dependency is introduced.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: For each drawn matrix the composite loop evaluates both the permanent and the determinant over the same field, from the same drawn entries, without redrawing.
- [hard] REQ-02: A test asserts the two quantities come from one draw: for a fixed address, the matrices the determinant sees are bit-identical to those the permanent sees.
- [hard] REQ-03: Each emitted shard record carries the determinant sample count and zero count over the matrices that shard drew, beside the permanent zero count for the same matrices.
- [hard] REQ-04: Each cell's pooled state carries the determinant sample count and zero count summed over that cell's shards.
- [hard] REQ-05: The determinant evaluation is switchable per cell from the campaign manifest, and a cell that runs without it records an explicit not-evaluated state rather than a numeric zero count, which would be indistinguishable from a cell that evaluated its matrices and found none singular.
- [hard] REQ-06: A test at a small $(q,n)$ whose matrices are exhaustively enumerable confirms the count the loop records equals the count obtained by recomputing the determinant matrix by matrix outside the loop over the same addresses.
- [hard] REQ-07: Adding the companion leaves permanent counts unchanged: a run with the companion enabled and one with it disabled produce identical permanent zero counts for the same addresses.
- [hard] REQ-08: The per-matrix wall-clock the companion adds is recorded per shard, so its measured cost is visible in the dataset rather than inferred.

## Notes

This work produces counts. Turning those counts into estimates, intervals and pass-or-fail verdicts is the acceptance layer's concern, and nothing here compares a measured determinant fraction against any reference value.

The permanent and determinant results are separate quantities pooled through one accumulator, so a cell that runs without the companion pools correctly rather than contributing a spurious zero.

No batch-parallel path exists in-tree for any field: the only parallel permanent routine splits one matrix's Gray-code walk and exists for $\mathbb{F}_3$ alone. A campaign needs both paths and chooses per cell from measurement; the choosing is the selection leaf's work, behind this one.

title: Processor backend selection for campaign cells
description:
The processor half of the campaign's backend selection: each cell reads its backend from the frozen manifest, and the scalar, batch-parallel, intra-matrix-parallel and generic Ryser paths are all reachable from that table.

## Background

Backend ranking in this problem family is measured, not intuited, and the measurements contradict the obvious expectation: from $n = 20$ upward at $q = 3$ the intra-matrix parallel path overtakes batch parallelism and leads by roughly a factor of two at $n = 24$ and $n = 28$. A campaign therefore needs both paths and must choose per $(q, n)$ from measurement, which is why the choice is read from the frozen manifest rather than computed.

Above the packed $\mathbb{F}_7$ kernel's $16$-lane ceiling the generic Ryser routine is the only processor path that remains; it is correct but reaches only $0.798$ matrices per second at $n = 24$, far under the rate a campaign cell needs. It stays reachable because a correct slow path is what a cell selects when nothing faster covers its size.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A cell's backend is read from the campaign manifest's per-$(q,n)$ table, and no code path selects a backend from a value observed during the run.
- [hard] REQ-02: The scalar single-word path is selectable for $q \in \{3,5,7\}$ where the manifest names it.
- [hard] REQ-03: The batch-parallel path is selectable for $q \in \{3,5,7\}$ where the manifest names it.
- [hard] REQ-04: The intra-matrix parallel path is selectable for $\mathbb{F}_3$ where the manifest names it.
- [hard] REQ-05: The generic Ryser path is selectable for any $(q,n)$ the packed kernels do not cover, so a cell above the packed $\mathbb{F}_7$ ceiling has a correct processor path.
- [hard] REQ-06: A backend the manifest names but the build does not provide halts that cell with an error naming the cell and the missing backend, rather than substituting another backend and continuing.

## Notes

Halting on an unavailable backend is specific to a preregistered campaign and is the explicit-failure arm of `@/inv/accelerator-safe-fallback`, not a breach of it: that invariant's tested-safe-fallback rule governs library capability dispatch, which this change does not touch, while a preregistered cell naming an absent backend is not a recoverable resource failure — a substituted backend would corrupt the frozen selection the dataset records, so the halt is kept explicit and named.

Cross-backend behavioural agreement is certified by the shared conformance suite leaf, not re-asserted here.

title: Accelerator execution for campaign cells
description:
The accelerator half of the campaign's execution layer — launches sized from measured per-matrix cost, exclusive device access, and defined behaviour when the device is absent.

## Background

Accelerator launch sizing is a wall-clock question rather than a memory question. Device memory is not the binding resource at any batch size in reach, while per-launch time scales as $M \cdot n \cdot 2^n / W$, so holding a batch size fixed while $n$ rises from $20$ to $24$ multiplies per-launch occupancy by $19.2$, and each further step of $4$ in $n$ costs about another factor of $19$. A batch size that occupies the device for a comfortable fraction of a second at one size occupies it for many seconds at the next. The best batch size measured is $M = 1024$; doubling to $M = 2048$ cost a $33\%$ loss in sustained rate at $q{=}3$, $n{=}24$, so the optimum within the tested set is interior.

Concurrency matters because a campaign runs three fields. Two executions contending for one device produce timings that describe the contention rather than the kernel, and the repository already provides a host lock wrapper for exactly this.

- [hard] REQ-03: Accelerator work and timed host work run under the repository's benchmark host lock wrapper (`dev/scripts/ccx1-bench-flock.sh`), so two concurrent field executions never contend for one device.
- [hard] REQ-04: A cell whose manifest names an accelerator backend on a host without the device halts that cell with an error naming the cell and the missing device, and never silently falls back to a processor path, since a substituted backend would break the frozen selection the dataset records.
- [hard] REQ-05: A build without accelerator support compiles and runs the processor-only campaign, with accelerator cells refusing rather than failing to build.

title: Standing acceptance tests for campaign cells
description:
Per-cell acceptance tests wired into the campaign driver: an exact test of the proved permanent floor, an exact two-sided test of the determinant companion, one global error budget across both families, and a halt-and-preserve rule with a predeclared retry policy.

## Background

The floor $\Pr[\mathrm{per}(A) = 0] \ge 1/q$ is proved for every $n$ at odd characteristic, so a cell significantly below $1/q$ indicts the pipeline rather than the mathematics, and such a cell can never be reported as a scientific finding. Running that check on every cell costs nothing and is sharper than small-$n$ enumeration anchors, which say nothing at the sizes a campaign cares about.

Its false-alarm rate has to be controlled or the check destroys itself. A nominal $95\%$ interval misses its parameter $5\%$ of the time and only the lower excursion trips a one-sided test, so a single cell sitting at $1/q$ — the worst case the theorem allows — flags with probability up to $2.5\%$; across a grid of $63$ cells that compounds to a $79\%$ chance of at least one false alarm, halting a healthy campaign nearly every run. The correction is an explicit family-wise error rate, and it must be allocated across both test families together rather than spending a fresh budget on each.

The determinant companion is checked against the exact finite-$n$ singular probability, never against its $n \to \infty$ limit. The limit overstates the exact value by $3.5 \times 10^{-3}$ at $q=3$, $n=4$ and by $3.8 \times 10^{-4}$ at $q=3$, $n=6$ — tens to hundreds of standard errors at cells that cost minutes to sample — so a limit-based check would manufacture failures exactly where the campaign's data is tightest.

Rerunning a halted cell until it passes spends the error budget silently, so retry behaviour is predeclared rather than decided in the moment.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: Each completed cell is checked against $\Pr[\mathrm{per}(A) = 0] \ge 1/q$ by a one-sided exact binomial test of the composite null evaluated at its worst case $p = 1/q$.
- [hard] REQ-02: Each completed cell for which the companion ran is checked by a two-sided exact binomial test of its determinant zero count against $1 - \prod_{i=1}^{n}(1 - q^{-i})$ at that cell's $q$ and $n$, and a cell whose determinant state is not-evaluated is skipped rather than tested against a count it does not have.
- [hard] REQ-03: The determinant reference value is computed per cell from the finite-$n$ product, and no code path compares a measured determinant fraction against an asymptotic limit.
- [hard] REQ-04: Each checked completed cell's estimate and interval, for both the permanent and the determinant, are computed here and recorded with the cell's verdict, so estimation and decision share one code path.
- [hard] REQ-05: The error budget is allocated across the permanent-floor family and the determinant family from one global total, with each family's share and each cell's resulting level fixed before any campaign matrix is drawn and recorded with the campaign.
- [hard] REQ-06: A failing cell halts the campaign, and the failure is recorded with the cell identity, counts, test statistic and level, rather than being reported as a scientific finding.
- [hard] REQ-07: A rerun after a halt is admitted only under the campaign's predeclared retry rule, which states what may be rerun, how many attempts are allowed, and how the error budget is charged; a rerun outside that rule is refused by the driver.
- [hard] REQ-08: A rejecting completed cell's data and verdict are preserved in the dataset together with the contradiction. A halted cell preserves every valid manifested shard completed before the halt as pooled raw counts plus its reason, carries no final estimate or verdict, and a later run neither removes nor overwrites either record.
- [hard] REQ-09: Acceptance decisions use exact tests only, taken through the log-scale or threshold-comparison interface so a decision stays correct where an exact tail underflows double precision; normal-approximation critical values appear nowhere in the decision path.
- [hard] REQ-10: A test drives the acceptance layer with synthetic counts that must halt and with counts that must pass, asserting the verdict and the recorded evidence in both cases, including at a sample size where the exact tail underflows.

## Notes

The proved upper bound $\Pr \le 1/q + 11/q^3$ is deliberately not part of the test: campaign cells sit tens to thousands of standard errors below it, so checking it would never fire and never inform.

planning.outcome: Per-cell exact binomial floor and determinant tests under one global error budget, halting on failure under a predeclared retry rule

title: Four-matrix batched AVX2 single-word path for $\mathbb{F}_3$ permanents
description:
Build the four-matrix batched single-word $\mathbb{F}_3$ permanent path that the kernel crate's batched arithmetic type was introduced for, and demonstrate it agrees with the scalar kernel matrix for matrix.

## Background

The AVX2 single-word $\mathbb{F}_3$ permanent kernel zero-pads one bipedal word into a four-element lane, so three lanes of four carry no data and the kernel runs slower than the scalar one — a committed cross-CPU receipt puts scalar at $0.317$–$0.319$ of the AVX2 time at $n \in \{16, 20, 24\}$.

The module documentation states the intended resolution explicitly: the AVX2 single-word kernel exists to exercise dispatch wiring and kernel correctness on real hardware, and "the batched multi-matrix path is the performance-oriented user". That user does not exist. The batched four-lane arithmetic type it refers to landed in the kernel crate as `Bipedal3x4` (`crates/gf2-kernels-simd/src/bipedal/bipedal3.rs:183`), and nothing in the algebra crate evaluates four matrices' permanents through it. Building it makes the AVX2 lanes carry four matrices instead of one, which is what the hardware was there for.

The placement is settled here, not by the implementer: the batched Gray-walk evaluation over `Bipedal3x4` is SIMD `unsafe` and therefore lands in the kernel crate beside the existing AVX2 permanent kernel (`crates/gf2-kernels-simd/src/x86/bipedal_avx2.rs`), per `@/inv/unsafe-kernel-isolation`; the algebra crate adds only the safe public entry point and packing glue over it.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A public entry point evaluates four $\mathbb{F}_3$ permanents at once through the batched bipedal type, returning one value per input matrix in input order.
- [hard] REQ-02: The batched path agrees with the scalar single-word kernel on a randomised conformance set covering each size where one bipedal word suffices, and on the committed computer-algebra reference vectors.
- [hard] REQ-03: A batch containing fewer than four matrices returns correct values for the matrices present, with a test covering each partial-batch width.
- [hard] REQ-04: The batched path joins the crate's shared permanent behavioural suite, so it is exercised by the same contract as every other permanent backend rather than by a private test set.
- [hard] REQ-05: Each modified SIMD source file has its sibling assembly artefact regenerated in the same change.
- [hard] REQ-06: The entry point is reachable on hosts without AVX2 through the crate's existing feature and runtime-detection conventions, with a test asserting the fallback returns the same values.

## Notes

This change adds a capability and asserts its correctness. Which path the public single-matrix dispatcher selects, and the prose and benchmark labels describing that selection, are a separate concern from whether the batched path exists and is correct.

title: Benchmark receipt for the batched $\mathbb{F}_3$ permanent path
description:

title: Timing receipt for the determinant companion at campaign sizes
description:
A committed measurement of the finite-field determinant's cost at campaign sizes beside the permanent's cost at the same sizes, so the companion's marginal expense is a measured ratio rather than an argument from complexity expressions.

## Background

The companion curve's affordability currently rests on arithmetic, not measurement: elimination is $O(n^3)$ per matrix against the permanent's $\Theta(n 2^n)$, so the work ratio goes as $n^2 / 2^n$ — roughly $4 \times 10^{-4}$ at $n = 20$ and $3 \times 10^{-6}$ at $n = 28$. That is arithmetic on the complexity expressions, and the constant factors, which differ between a bit-sliced Gray-code walk and an elimination over $\mathbb{F}_q$, are unknown.

The determinant path exists and is usable: `FieldMatrix::det` (`crates/gf2-core/src/field/inverse.rs:494`) is generic over the finite-field trait and sits below the algebra crate. Existing benchmarks for it cover a different field and much larger sizes — $n \in \{64, 256, 1024\}$ over a Mersenne prime field and a binary extension field — so no committed receipt times it over $\mathbb{F}_3$, $\mathbb{F}_5$ or $\mathbb{F}_7$ at the sizes this campaign uses. The repository requires performance claims to rest on committed measurements, so the companion is timed before it is assumed cheap.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A committed receipt reports wall-clock per matrix for the finite-field determinant over $\mathbb{F}_3$, $\mathbb{F}_5$ and $\mathbb{F}_7$ at the sizes the campaign grid reaches for each field, spanning at least $n \in \{4, 12, 20\}$ and each field's frontier size.
- [hard] REQ-02: The same receipt reports measured permanent cost per matrix at the same $(q, n)$ on a campaign-candidate backend, so the companion's marginal cost is stated as a measured ratio.
- [hard] REQ-03: The receipt records seeds, git revision, hardware and toolchain, and reports repetition counts with dispersion rather than a single timing.
- [hard] REQ-04: The receipt states, per cell, whether adding the determinant companion fits the campaign's per-cell wall-clock budget, and names the cells where it does not.
- [hard] REQ-05: Rate ratios are formed from pooled totals rather than by averaging per-repetition reciprocals.
- [hard] REQ-06: Where the measured ratio contradicts the complexity-based estimate, both are recorded together with the contradiction.

This work measures cost and changes no evaluation path: the determinant routine, its supporting elimination, and the permanent kernels all exist, and how the companion is wired into a campaign run is a separate concern.

title: Re-measurement of contested backend orderings before the freeze
description:
Replicated timing of four named backend configurations — the one comparison the feasibility measurements left unresolved, and each field's frontier-cell selection — producing the receipted ordering a frozen campaign backend table can rest on.

## Background

One cell's ordering is explicitly open. At $q = 3$, $n = 28$ the accelerator path at $M = 1024$ and the intra-matrix parallel path differ by $1.6\%$ with the parallel path ahead, but each rate is a single cell execution. Within one execution repetitions are very stable — repetition dispersion is $0.12\%$ for the parallel path and $0.16\%$ for the accelerator — while across independent executions of one configuration the spread reaches $1.80\%$ with a median of $0.84\%$. The gap is therefore comparable to the widest disagreement measured across re-executions, and no ordering is asserted; the feasibility study states that a campaign choosing that cell's backend should re-measure.

The rest of the scope is fixed by which cells the campaign's frontier actually rests on. At a standard error of $10^{-3}$ the frontier is $n = 28$ at $q = 3$, $n = 24$ at $q = 5$ and $n = 20$ at $q = 7$, and the envelope's selected paths there are intra-matrix rayon at $19.58$ matrices per second, batch rayon at $11.83$, and the accelerator at $M = 1024$ at $57.93$. Those are the rates every per-cell sample size was derived from, so they are the ones a campaign cannot afford to have wrong.

A published headline elsewhere in the repository is contradicted by newer measurement of the same configurations: an accelerator speedup of $28.65\times$ at $n = 24$ and $30.32\times$ at $n = 28$ reproduces only against a single-thread AVX2 baseline, and restating it against the best measured processor path gives $0.46\times$ and $0.44\times$.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: Exactly four configurations are measured, and no others: $(q{=}3,\; n{=}28,\; \text{accelerator},\; M{=}1024)$; $(q{=}3,\; n{=}28,\; \text{intra-matrix rayon})$; $(q{=}5,\; n{=}24,\; \text{batch rayon})$; and $(q{=}7,\; n{=}20,\; \text{accelerator},\; M{=}1024)$.
- [hard] REQ-02: Each configuration is executed at least $12$ times, each execution a fresh process on a quiesced host. Taking the recorded worst-case cross-execution disagreement of $1.80\%$ between two executions as implying a per-execution standard deviation near $1.27\%$, twelve executions put the standard error of a difference of means near $0.52\%$, so the contested $1.6\%$ gap sits about three standard errors out.
- [hard] REQ-03: Executions are interleaved across configurations rather than run in per-configuration blocks, so thermal drift over the measurement window cannot be confounded with the configuration being compared.
- [hard] REQ-04: The $q = 3$, $n = 28$ comparison reports a separation verdict: either one configuration leads at the stated confidence, or the receipt states that the two remain unseparated at the replication achieved and the frozen table records the basis on which its choice was nonetheless made.
- [hard] REQ-05: Each configuration reports within-execution repetition dispersion and across-execution dispersion as separate quantities.
- [hard] REQ-06: Timed windows run under the repository's benchmark host lock, so no other work shares the device or the cores during a measurement.
- [hard] REQ-07: Rates are composite rates covering draw, pack, evaluate and count, not kernel-only rates, and each is formed from pooled totals rather than by averaging per-repetition reciprocals.
- [hard] REQ-08: Each configuration's re-measured rate is reported beside the single-execution rate the envelope used, and a disagreement wider than the measured cross-execution dispersion is recorded as a contradiction rather than silently replacing the earlier figure.
- [hard] REQ-09: The receipt records seeds, stream addresses, matrix counts per execution, git revision, hardware and toolchain.

## Notes

Configurations outside this list are out of scope. A backend enters a campaign's selectable set only once a committed measurement covers it at the cells where it would be chosen, whether that measurement comes from here or from a separately receipted accelerator study.

title: Scientific preregistration protocol for the campaign
description:
The preregistration document that fixes what the campaign estimates, on which cells, at what sample sizes, under what error budget, with what failure and exclusion rules — written and committed before any campaign matrix is drawn.

## Background

The conjecture under study is asymptotic: $\Pr[\mathrm{per}(A) = 0] = 1/q + o(1)$ is a statement about $n \to \infty$, and no finite grid of $n$ can confirm or contradict it in either direction, since an asymptotic statement is compatible with any finite prefix of the sequence. What finite data can address is the finite-$n$ correction $\delta(n) = \Pr[\mathrm{per}(A) = 0] - 1/q$ — its sign, its magnitude, and how it varies with $n$ and $q$ — and the pipeline that measures it.

The proved results bound that quantity far too loosely to substitute for measurement. The floor $\Pr \ge 1/q$ holds for every $n$ at odd characteristic; the ceiling $\Pr \le 1/q + 11/q^3$ holds for $n \ge 3$ but sits $0.03$ to $0.41$ above the floor, between one-and-a-half and three-and-a-half orders of magnitude looser than the deviations a campaign can resolve.

Preregistration is what separates this campaign from the by-product statistics that preceded it. Those cells had no fixed sample size and no stopping rule, and one of them — a $q = 7$, $n = 20$ reading $2.30$ standard errors below the floor — is exactly the shape of result that a post-hoc threshold manufactures. An earlier revision of the feasibility study spent its top recommendation chasing an apparent below-floor signal that proved to be two measurement defects plus fluctuation.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The estimand is stated as $\delta(n) = \Pr[\mathrm{per}(A) = 0] - 1/q$ over the measured range, with the explicit record that no finite grid tests an asymptotic statement in either direction.
- [hard] REQ-02: $N$ per cell is fixed from the measured envelope before any campaign matrix is drawn and is not revised in response to observed values, and no stopping rule is keyed on the observed statistic.
- [hard] REQ-03: The cell universe names a core processor-feasible grid — all $n$ from $4$ to the per-$q$ frontier, the frontier at a standard error of $10^{-3}$ being $n = 28$ at $q = 3$, $n = 24$ at $q = 5$ and $n = 20$ at $q = 7$, giving $K = 63$ cells — together with any predeclared accelerator-contingent extension cells.
- [hard] REQ-04: Extension cells either enter the multiplicity accounting with the core grid or are placed in an explicitly gatekept second family whose entry condition is stated before any draw.
- [hard] REQ-05: A global error budget is allocated numerically across the permanent-floor family and the determinant family, and the per-cell level each family uses follows from that allocation.
- [hard] REQ-06: Acceptance decisions are specified as exact binomial tests — one-sided against the composite null $\Pr \ge 1/q$ evaluated at $p = 1/q$, and two-sided against $1 - \prod_{i=1}^{n}(1 - q^{-i})$ — with normal-approximation critical values recorded as planning approximations only.
- [hard] REQ-07: Exclusion and failure rules are predeclared: what halts a cell, what quarantines a shard, what may be rerun, how many attempts are permitted, and how a rerun charges the error budget.
- [hard] REQ-08: Backend selection is specified as a function of correctness, safety and measured throughput alone, and explicitly never of an observed zero fraction.
- [hard] REQ-09: The $q = 7$, $n = 20$ cell is committed as the first cell resampled under a preregistered $N$, and the by-product reading motivating that choice stays on the record whatever the resample returns.
- [hard] REQ-10: The validation plan names the exact enumeration anchors — $q = 3$ up to $n = 4$, $q = 5$ and $q = 7$ up to $n = 3$ — and requires sampler and estimator agreement with them before any estimated cell is believed.
- [hard] REQ-11: The $q = 3$ arm is framed as reproduction and precision against published numerics, with no wording implying the campaign extends the $q = 3$ curve in $n$.
- [hard] REQ-12: The convergence-shape comparison is preregistered as a likelihood comparison on observed counts under their binomial sampling distribution, with the range of $n$ over which candidate families are distinguishable reported rather than assumed.
- [hard] REQ-13: Novelty statements are conditional on the recorded literature search, naming what was searched, what it returned, and that search's stated limits.
- [hard] REQ-14: The protocol defines a cell's terminal states — completed only with every manifested shard, exactly its preregistered $N$, and final estimates and verdicts; or halted with its reason while the summary preserves every valid manifested shard completed before the halt as pooled raw counts but no final estimates or verdicts — so a cell that is neither is an incomplete campaign rather than a silent omission.

## Notes

The protocol is published at the dataset home rather than in an issue-scoped area, since it must outlive the work that produced it and be readable beside the data it governs.

This document carries forward the campaign-design half of the feasibility study's mandate. The study fixed the attainable envelope and closed with a go recommendation and a campaign design; the design is not a finished artefact until it is stated as a protocol that binds a specific campaign, with its cell universe, sample sizes, error budget and failure rules committed in advance. Delivery of the study itself is credited to the completed study work; this document is the contribution that re-validates its design half against what the campaign will actually run, and revises it where measurement since has moved.

## References

The protocol cites [GGK2025], [HKS2026], and [Scheinerman2024] through the repository citation registry.

title: Frozen root manifest for the campaign
description:
The immutable root manifest instance for one campaign: the complete cell universe, the sample size per cell, the multiplicity count, the stream purpose namespace, the shard identities, and the backend chosen for each cell — committed before the first campaign matrix is drawn.

## Background

Preregistration only binds if it is instantiated. A protocol states the rules; the manifest states the numbers those rules produce for one campaign, and freezing it is what makes the difference between a fixed sample size and a sample size chosen once the data looked interesting.

The manifest is also the campaign's single addressing authority. Stream allocation must be structurally disjoint rather than coincidentally so: an earlier round in this problem family allocated sustained runs from a base commensurate with the grid's own allocation, so the two ranges collided in index space and the pooled counts were valid only because no colliding pair happened to share a cell. That was verified rather than designed, and a campaign running twelve hours per cell cannot audit its way out of the same mistake.

Every backend in the table has to be one whose ordering at that cell rests on committed measurement. Two measurement inputs feed the table: a re-measurement of the backends already present in the workspace, and whichever accelerator configurations a separate accelerator study retains and receipts. A configuration with no committed measurement at the cells where it would be chosen does not enter the table, however promising it looks.

- [hard] REQ-01: A committed root manifest instance enumerates the complete $(q, n)$ cell universe, $N$ per cell, the cell count entering the multiplicity adjustment, the stream purpose namespace with each purpose's tag, the shard identities per cell, and the backend selected per cell.

title: Permanental rank-deficiency predicate with exact validation
description:
A predicate deciding permanental rank deficiency of a rectangular matrix over $\mathbb{F}_q$, validated by exhaustive enumeration and by agreement with an independent brute-force routine sharing no code path with it.

## Background

The rectangular event in the literature is permanental rank deficiency, not the vanishing of a rectangular permanent. For an $n \times k$ matrix $A$ with $k \le n$,

$$
\mathrm{per\text{-}rank}(A) < k
\iff
\text{each } k \times k \text{ row submatrix of } A \text{ has zero permanent},
$$

so the predicate is a conjunction over the $\binom{n}{k}$ row subsets. A single scalar "rectangular permanent" is not the quantity at all: it can vanish through cancellation while some $k \times k$ submatrix has nonzero permanent, and it can be nonzero when the rank condition is what one wants to test. Testing the event therefore needs no new numeric kernel — it enumerates row subsets and reuses the existing square kernels, exiting at the first nonzero permanent, which is the overwhelmingly common case.

No permanental-rank routine exists in the workspace today; the public permanent surface is square-only, exactly seven functions plus three accelerator batch entry points, all taking square matrices.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A predicate decides, for an $n \times k$ matrix over $\mathbb{F}_q$ with $k \le n$, whether $\mathrm{per\text{-}rank}(A) < k$, by testing $k \times k$ row submatrices and exiting at the first nonzero permanent.
- [hard] REQ-02: An independent brute-force permanental-rank routine, sharing no code path with the predicate, is available as an oracle.
- [hard] REQ-03: Exhaustive enumeration over the $q^{nk}$ matrices confirms the predicate and the oracle return the same decision on every matrix for at least $(q,n,k) \in \{(3,3,1),(3,3,2),(3,4,2),(5,3,2),(7,3,2)\}$.
- [hard] REQ-04: The predicate's decision is correct on hand-constructed matrices covering the boundary cases: a zero row, a zero column, $k = 1$, $k = n$, and a matrix whose scalar rectangular permanent vanishes while a $k \times k$ submatrix permanent does not.
- [hard] REQ-05: Documentation states that permanental rank deficiency is the conjunction over row submatrices, and that a vanishing rectangular permanent is a different quantity.
- [hard] REQ-06: Documentation states that the $(n,k)$ pairs reachable by sampling lie outside the $k \le 0.1\sqrt{n}$ hypothesis of the cited theorem, so agreement supports the implementation rather than the theorem in its proven range.
- [hard] REQ-07: The predicate carries no dependency on statistical machinery: it decides one matrix and reports nothing about rates.

## Notes

The proved regime is unreachable by direct sampling. The theorem requires $k \le 0.1\sqrt{n}$, so even $k = 3$ needs $n \ge 900$, where the event probability is about $3 \cdot 3^{-900}$; the predicate's role in the campaign is as a correctness check, not as a test of the theorem.

planning.outcome: Permanental rank-deficiency predicate over row submatrices, agreeing with an independent oracle on exhaustive enumeration

title: Observable-event rate estimates for permanental rank deficiency
description:
Stochastic estimates of the permanental rank-deficiency rate at the small $k$ where the event is observable, checked against the values those cases are known to take, together with a measured cost profile for the predicate.

## Background

Direct estimation of permanental rank deficiency is confined to small $k$. At $k = 1$ the event is an all-zero column, with probability exactly $q^{-n}$ — about $169$ events per $10^{7}$ samples at $q = 3$, $n = 10$. At $k = 2$ the predicted rate is about $2q^{-n}$, similarly observable at moderate $n$. Beyond that the event probability falls as $k/q^{n}$ and no Monte Carlo campaign observes it.

These estimates are a pipeline check rather than a test of the cited theorem, whose hypothesis $k \le 0.1\sqrt{n}$ no observable $(n,k)$ satisfies, and they must say so. Their statistical treatment is the small-count regime: event counts are in the tens, where a normal-approximation interval is at its weakest, so exact intervals are used.

The predicate's cost profile is measured here rather than asserted. Its early exit is the reason testing the event needs no new kernel, and the claim that expected work per matrix is a small constant number of $k \times k$ permanents rather than $\binom{n}{k}$ of them is a measurement the repository requires to be receipted.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: An estimate of $\Pr[\mathrm{per\text{-}rank} < k]$ at $k = 1$ over at least three $(q, n)$ cells agrees with the exact $q^{-n}$, with agreement stated as an exact interval containing the exact value at a stated sample size and level.
- [hard] REQ-02: An estimate at $k = 2$ over at least two $(q, n)$ cells is reported with its exact interval beside the $\approx 2q^{-n}$ heuristic, and any disagreement is recorded rather than reconciled.
- [hard] REQ-03: Intervals are exact rather than normal-approximation, since event counts are in the tens.
- [hard] REQ-04: A committed receipt reports the measured mean number of $k \times k$ permanent evaluations per matrix at each measured $(q, n, k)$, confirming or contradicting that the early exit keeps expected work a small constant.
- [hard] REQ-05: The receipt records seeds, stream addresses, sample sizes, git revision, hardware and toolchain, so each estimate is regenerable.
- [hard] REQ-06: Draws come from a stream purpose distinct from every campaign cell's, so no validation draw can enter a published zero-fraction cell.
- [hard] REQ-07: The report of these estimates states that the measured $(n,k)$ lie outside the $k \le 0.1\sqrt{n}$ hypothesis, so agreement supports the implementation and the $k/q^{n}$ heuristic rather than the theorem in its proven range.

## Notes

An estimate that disagrees with its known value is a pipeline finding, not a mathematical one, and is recorded as such.

title: Exact enumeration anchors for the smallest cells
description:
Exact ground truth for the smallest cells, computed by exhaustive enumeration and living where a campaign can re-run it, with the sampler and the estimator checked against it before any estimated cell is believed.

## Background

For the smallest sizes the zero fraction is computable exactly by enumerating all $q^{n^2}$ matrices: $q = 3$ up to $n = 4$ ($3^{16} \approx 4.3 \times 10^7$), and $q = 5$ and $q = 7$ up to $n = 3$ ($5^9 \approx 2.0 \times 10^6$ and $7^9 \approx 4.0 \times 10^7$). These give ground truth against which a sampler and an estimator are validated rather than trusted.

Anchors of this kind exist today, but in the wrong place. The order-3 permanent anchor script, the determinant anchor script, their committed outputs, and a standalone anchor-report crate all live under a study directory in an issue-scoped documentation area, so they are archival candidates attached to work that has closed. A campaign that must re-run its anchors needs them in a permanent home.

The determinant anchor is worth the same treatment and is stronger than the permanent anchor where it applies: the count of invertible $n \times n$ matrices over $\mathbb{F}_q$ is $\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}(q^n - q^k)$, giving the exact singular probability $1 - \prod_{i=1}^{n}(1 - q^{-i})$ at every finite $n$ — for instance $11/27$ at $q = 3$, $n = 2$ and $313/729$ at $n = 3$. Unlike the order-3 permanent anchors, it pins a value at every size the campaign measures.

- [hard] REQ-03: Enumerated permanent values agree with the previously committed order-3 anchor counts for $q \in \{3,5,7\}$, and any disagreement is recorded with both readings.

title: Campaign arm for $q = 5$
description:
Execution of the frozen $q = 5$ cells: drawn from their allocated streams, evaluated on their assigned backends, emitted as dataset shards with a field summary, and driven to a recorded terminal state cell by cell.

## Background

A campaign arm executes cells that a frozen manifest already fixed: the sizes, the sample size per cell, the stream addresses, and the backend are inputs, not decisions taken while running. The arm's job is to draw the matrices those addresses name, evaluate their permanents and the determinant companion where the manifest enables it, pool the counts, and record the terminal state of every cell it is responsible for.

Two terminal states are admissible for a cell, and no third. A cell is *completed*: every manifested shard is present, exactly its preregistered $N$ is pooled, and its final estimates and acceptance verdicts are recorded. Or a cell is *halted*: every valid manifested shard completed before the halt remains as pooled raw counts, possibly as a non-prefix subset, its reason is recorded, and it carries no final estimates or verdicts. A cell that is simply missing — neither completed nor halted — is neither a result nor a falsification, and leaves the arm incomplete.

Every completed cell is checked against the proved floor $\Pr[\mathrm{per}(A) = 0] \ge 1/q$. A cell below that floor indicts the pipeline rather than the mathematics and halts the arm for investigation; it is never reported as a scientific finding.

The scientific reach is bounded by resolution rather than by size. Published $q = 3$ numerics stop being distinguishable from $1/3$ beyond $n = 13$, and this budget's per-cell sample sizes sit between $0.7\times$ and $2.3\times$ those across the measured sizes — the same order, not a different regime. Expect the deviation $\delta(n)$ to be characterised only around $n \lesssim 14$ to $16$ and bounded above that.

The $q = 5$ arm is one of the two fields for which a recorded literature search found no published numerics, so its cells are the campaign's novel measurements rather than a reproduction.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: Each $q = 5$ cell named in the frozen manifest reaches a terminal recorded state — completed with every manifested shard, exactly its preregistered $N$, and final estimates and verdicts; or halted with any unique manifested shard subset, including none, pooled as raw counts plus its reason and no final estimates or verdicts — and no cell is left in neither state.
- [hard] REQ-02: The arm draws only from the streams the frozen manifest allocates to it, and runs no cell at an $N$ other than the frozen one and no cell absent from the frozen manifest.
- [hard] REQ-03: Per-shard records land under this field's shard paths and this field's summary under the campaign id, and the arm writes no file outside its own field's paths.
- [hard] REQ-04: The field summary states, for each frozen cell of this field, its terminal state and pooled permanent and determinant counts; completed cells additionally carry estimates with intervals and applicable acceptance verdicts, while halted cells carry no final estimates or verdicts.
- [hard] REQ-05: A rejecting completed cell's data and verdict remain in the dataset. A halted cell's raw counts from any unique manifested shard subset, including none, and its reason remain without final estimates or verdicts, and a later run neither removes nor overwrites either record.

title: Campaign arm for $q = 7$
description:

## Background

A campaign arm executes cells that a frozen manifest already fixed: the sizes, the sample size per cell, the stream addresses, and the backend are inputs, not decisions taken while running. title: Deterministic finalization of a completed campaign dataset
description:
A finalizer that runs once every field has finished: it pools the per-field summaries into the campaign summary, verifies the dataset is complete and internally consistent, and writes the checksum file covering the raw data set.

## Background

Field executions run independently and each writes only its own paths, so nothing in the dataset pools across fields while they are running — that is what lets them run concurrently without a shared writer. The pooled campaign summary and the checksum file are therefore campaign-scoped artefacts with exactly one writer, and this is it.

The checksum boundary matters as much as the checksums. The raw data set — root manifest, shard records, field summaries, and the pooled summary — is what a reader must be able to verify. Derived artefacts such as the analysis report, generated figures, and model-comparison outputs quote those numbers and sometimes quote the checksums themselves, so including them would make the checksum file depend on documents that depend on it. Keeping the boundary explicit avoids that cycle and makes "verify the data I was given" a well-defined operation.

Finalization is also the campaign's completeness check. A dataset whose cells are partly completed, partly halted and partly missing is not a finished campaign, and the difference between a halted cell and an absent one is the difference between a recorded falsification and a gap.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The finalizer pools every field summary into one campaign `summary.csv` carrying, per $(q,n)$, the pooled permanent and determinant counts and terminal state. Completed rows carry point estimates with intervals and applicable acceptance verdicts; halted rows carry their reason and leave every final estimate and verdict empty.
- [hard] REQ-02: Finalization is deterministic: running it twice on one dataset produces byte-identical outputs, and the pooled result does not depend on the order fields finished or the order files are read.
- [hard] REQ-03: The finalizer refuses to finalize a dataset in which a cell named by the frozen manifest has no terminal record, naming every such cell.
- [hard] REQ-04: The finalizer verifies that per-shard records agree with the field summaries that pooled them, and refuses on any disagreement rather than overwriting either.
- [hard] REQ-05: `checksums.sha256` covers exactly the raw data set — root manifest, shard records, field summaries, and the pooled summary — and covers no derived artefact.
- [hard] REQ-06: A verification path re-checks a finalized dataset against its checksum file and reports pass or the failing paths.
- [hard] REQ-07: The finalizer writes only campaign-scoped paths and modifies no field-scoped file, so finalizing cannot alter the data it summarises.
- [hard] REQ-08: Outputs carry data and mechanical provenance only, with no interpretive statement about what the pooled numbers mean.

## Notes

A campaign that halted under its predeclared rule finalizes normally: the halt is a recorded terminal state, and the resulting dataset is a complete record of a falsified run rather than an incomplete one.
