title: Curve and table generation pipeline
description:
A reusable pipeline that turns completed cells in any published-format campaign dataset into estimate tables with interval columns, zero-fraction curves against matrix size, and comparison columns against published prior art, while retaining halted cells' partial raw counts and reasons without synthesizing estimates or verdicts.

## Background

The repository already carries a permanent-domain plot generator and a set of reproduction wrappers for this problem family, so figure generation has a precedent to sit beside rather than a convention to invent. What it must add is the discipline the repository requires of every Monte Carlo artefact: each estimate states its sample count and interval, and every plot or table carries error bars or interval columns.

The comparison against published $q = 3$ numerics is a first-class output rather than a remark. The right comparison is achieved precision, not trial count: matching the published sample sizes is not a goal, resolving $\delta(n) = p(n) - 1/q$ is. The published table gives point estimates without uncertainty, so supplying uncertainty metadata for every published-source cell — exact/no-sampling-uncertainty bounds for exact rows and, by reanalysis, Wilson intervals for Monte Carlo counts — is a contribution independent of how many samples any campaign draws.

This is tooling. It is developed and tested against fixture datasets in the published format, so its correctness does not wait on a campaign finishing, and it can be re-run against any later campaign.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The pipeline reads a dataset in the campaign's published format and emits the pooled sample count, point estimate $\hat p$, and $95\%$ Wilson interval for each completed $(q,n)$; a halted row emits its pooled raw counts and reason with no estimate, interval, or verdict.
- [hard] REQ-02: Curves of completed-cell $\hat p$ against $n$ per field carry interval error bars, and no emitted figure or table states an estimate without its sample count and its interval.
- [hard] REQ-03: Comparison columns for a completed cell against published $q = 3$ counts carry the published point estimate, the source row's exact/no-sampling-uncertainty representation or Wilson interval obtained by reanalysis of its Monte Carlo counts, the dataset's own interval, and a precision classification. A halted counterpart carries raw counts and reason but no estimate-based comparison.
- [hard] REQ-04: A completed cell whose interval excludes a published point estimate is flagged in the output rather than smoothed over.
- [hard] REQ-05: The pipeline refuses a dataset whose checksums do not verify, and refuses a dataset whose cells lack terminal states, rather than plotting from a tree it cannot vouch for.
- [hard] REQ-06: The pipeline runs from the dataset alone with no value transcribed by hand, and rerunning it against an unchanged dataset reproduces byte-identical outputs.
- [hard] REQ-07: Emitted figures and tables carry no interpretive text, so the wording of conclusions lives in an analysis narrative rather than in generated artefacts.
- [hard] REQ-08: Committed fixture datasets in the published format, including one with a halted cell and one with a checksum mismatch, exercise the pipeline's outputs and its refusals in an automated test.

## Notes

Outputs are keyed by campaign id so results from two campaigns never overwrite one another.

title: Analysis report on the measured zero-fraction curves
description:
The campaign's analysis report: what the measured curves show at the sizes measured, how they sit against the proved floor and the conjectured limit, what is reproduction and what is new, and what the pipeline's own checks returned.

## Background

The report is where interpretation lives, and it is the only place it lives: emitted datasets and generated figures carry data and mechanical provenance only. That separation exists because the alternative was measured — an earlier review cycle in this problem family regenerated receipts every time a claim's wording changed, and that was its largest single source of rework.

Two disciplines constrain the wording. Consistency with $1/q + o(1)$ can only be phrased at the measured sizes, because an asymptotic statement is compatible with any finite prefix of the sequence; and novelty for $q \in \{5, 7\}$ can only be stated conditionally on the recorded literature search, which ran one general web index rather than a bibliographic database and left three close candidate counting papers unread.

The report also inherits a live contradiction to resolve on the record rather than silently: an accelerator speedup headline of roughly $28$ to $30\times$ published elsewhere in the repository rests on a single-thread AVX2 baseline, and the same configurations restated against the best measured processor path give $0.46\times$ at $n = 24$ and $0.44\times$ at $n = 28$.

title: Convergence-shape model comparison for the deviation term
description:
A preregistered comparison between candidate shapes for the finite-size deviation $\delta(n) = \Pr[\mathrm{per}(A) = 0] - 1/q$, computed as a likelihood on the observed counts and published as its own artefact.

## Background

The campaign's measurable target is the shape of $\delta(n)$, and two families were named in advance as candidates: geometric decay $\delta \sim c\,q^{-\alpha n}$ and polynomial decay $\delta \sim c\,n^{-\beta}$. What a campaign can falsify is a model of $\delta(n)$; what it cannot falsify is either the asymptotic conjecture or the proved floor.

The comparison is computed on counts rather than on point estimates. Each cell is a binomial observation with a known sample size, so the likelihood of a candidate shape is available directly; fitting point estimates by weighted least squares and comparing by an information criterion discards that structure and misstates the uncertainty, particularly at cells whose counts are small relative to their sample size.

The honest limit is stated with the result: two families can be told apart only while $|\delta(n)|$ exceeds a few standard errors at several sizes, and the achievable precision means that range is expected to be roughly $n \lesssim 14$ to $16$.

## Success Criteria

- [aspirational] REQ-01: Candidate families $\delta(n) \sim c\,q^{-\alpha n}$ and $\delta(n) \sim c\,n^{-\beta}$ are compared by a likelihood computed on the observed zero counts under their binomial sampling distribution, not by weighted least squares on point estimates.
- [aspirational] REQ-02: The comparison specification — families, parameterisation, cells included, and comparison statistic — is fixed before the comparison is run against campaign data.
- [aspirational] REQ-03: The range of $n$ over which $|\delta(n)|$ exceeds a stated multiple of its standard error is reported, and no model preference is claimed outside that range.
- [aspirational] REQ-04: Parameter estimates carry intervals, and the result states whether each family's interval excludes the other family's behaviour.
- [aspirational] REQ-05: The outcome is recorded whatever it is, including an outcome in which the data do not distinguish the families.
- [aspirational] REQ-06: The comparison runs from the finalized dataset alone, is rerunnable from it, and records the campaign id and dataset checksum it used.
- [aspirational] REQ-07: The result is published as its own document with its own fit tables, and modifies no other published artefact.

## Notes

Every criterion here is aspirational: the deliverable is a characterisation whose informativeness is set by the precision the campaign achieves, which is bounded by measurement rather than by effort.

This artefact stands alone. A campaign report may cite it where it exists, and is complete without it; nothing in the hard contract waits on this comparison. Like every derived product, it sits outside the dataset's raw checksum set.

title: Permanental against determinantal zero-fraction comparison figure

The contrast is the point of the whole question. Two framings must not be confused. This figure compares zero fractions, which is what the campaign measures; a whole-distribution uniformity comparison between permanent and determinant values is a different question belonging to separate prior work in this repository.

title: Preregistered rare-event estimator design
description:
The design document for a rare-event estimator of the permanental rank-deficiency probability: proposal distribution, weighting, the unbiasedness argument, the validation plan, and the stream purposes it will draw from — written before any estimator code exists.

## Background

Direct sampling cannot reach the regime the cited theorem describes. The proved statement requires $k \le 0.1\sqrt{n}$, so even $k = 3$ needs $n \ge 900$, where the deficiency probability is about $k \cdot q^{-n}$ — of order $3 \cdot 3^{-900}$, which no Monte Carlo campaign observes at any budget. Direct estimation is confined to $k = 1$, where the event is an all-zero column with probability exactly $q^{-n}$, and $k = 2$, where the predicted rate is about $2q^{-n}$.

An importance-sampling or splitting estimator can extend that reach, and the danger it introduces is precisely that its output is unfalsifiable by inspection: a biased estimator or an interval with the wrong coverage produces a confident number about an event nobody can otherwise check. Fixing the estimator and its validation plan before writing it is what makes the later demonstration meaningful rather than a search for a configuration that agrees.

## Success Criteria

- [aspirational] REQ-01: The document specifies the proposal distribution and the weighting, in enough detail that two implementers would produce the same estimator.
- [aspirational] REQ-02: The unbiasedness argument is stated, identifying the conditions the proposal must satisfy for the weighted estimator to be unbiased.
- [aspirational] REQ-03: The variance behaviour is discussed, including how effective sample size will be reported and what would count as an unusable configuration.
- [aspirational] REQ-04: The validation plan names the exactly known cases the estimator will be checked against, the number of repeated runs, the nominal interval level, and the criterion by which coverage will be judged adequate.
- [aspirational] REQ-05: The target $(q, n, k)$ beyond direct sampling's reach is named in advance, with the reason direct sampling cannot reach it stated numerically.
- [aspirational] REQ-06: A distinct stream purpose is reserved for rare-event draws, so no such draw can enter a published zero-fraction cell.
- [aspirational] REQ-07: The document states the gap between the regime the estimator targets and the theorem's $k \le 0.1\sqrt{n}$ hypothesis numerically.

## Notes

Every criterion here is aspirational: whether a usable estimator exists for this event at these field orders is itself an open question, and a design concluding that none is available at this budget is a legitimate outcome.

title: Rare-event estimator with demonstrated unbiasedness and coverage
description:
The rare-event estimator built to its preregistered design, with unbiasedness and interval coverage demonstrated against exactly known cases.

## Background

A rare-event estimator's output cannot be checked by looking at it: the events it estimates are ones direct sampling never observes. Its credibility comes entirely from behaving correctly where the answer is known. At $k = 1$ the deficiency probability is exactly $q^{-n}$ at every $n$, and small $(q, n, k)$ are exhaustively enumerable, which gives a ladder of cases with known answers running from trivially small up to the edge of what direct sampling can reach.

Coverage is a separate property from unbiasedness and is demonstrated separately: an estimator can be unbiased while reporting intervals that contain the true value far less often than their nominal level claims, and it is the interval that a reader of the result will rely on.

## Success Criteria

- [aspirational] REQ-01: The estimator implements the preregistered proposal and weighting, and a test asserts the implemented weights match the specification on hand-checked cases.
- [aspirational] REQ-02: Unbiasedness is demonstrated against cases whose probability is known exactly, with the estimator's mean over repeated independent runs agreeing with the exact value within its own interval.
- [aspirational] REQ-03: Interval coverage is demonstrated empirically: over repeated runs at a stated nominal level, the fraction of intervals containing the exact value matches the nominal level within its own binomial interval.
- [aspirational] REQ-04: A deviation from the preregistered design made during implementation is recorded with its reason, and the validation is judged against the design as amended rather than silently against the new behaviour.
- [aspirational] REQ-05: Draws come from the reserved rare-event stream purpose, so no such draw can enter a published zero-fraction cell.
- [aspirational] REQ-06: A configuration whose effective sample size falls below the design's usability threshold is reported as unusable rather than as an estimate.

## Notes

Every criterion here is aspirational. A demonstrated failure to achieve coverage is a recorded result and closes this work honestly; it is not a reason to relax the criterion.

The estimate at the preregistered beyond-reach target is separate work behind this leaf on a dependency edge, producing its own receipted artefact.

title: Preregistered rare-event estimate beyond direct sampling
description:
The validated rare-event estimator produces one estimate at the preregistered target $(q, n, k)$ beyond direct sampling's reach, published as its own receipted artefact.

## Background

The estimate is the point of the estimator, and it is also the number nobody can check directly — which is why it lands only after the estimator's unbiasedness and coverage are demonstrated, and why the run's own diagnostics travel with it. An estimate that cannot state its variance and effective sample size is a number, not a result.

The artefact is a derived product: like every derived artefact it sits outside the dataset's raw checksum set and modifies no published raw file.

## Success Criteria

- [aspirational] REQ-01: One estimate is produced at the preregistered target $(q, n, k)$, reporting its variance and effective sample size beside the estimate itself.
- [aspirational] REQ-02: The artefact records the estimator configuration, the reserved rare-event stream purpose its draws came from, the seeds, the git revision, and the toolchain, so the run is reproducible from the artefact alone.
- [aspirational] REQ-03: A run whose effective sample size falls below the design's usability threshold is recorded as unusable rather than as an estimate, and that outcome closes this work honestly.
- [aspirational] REQ-04: The artefact is its own document under the campaign home, outside the raw checksum set, and modifies no other published artefact.

## Notes

Every criterion here is aspirational: whether the preregistered target is reachable at a usable effective sample size is exactly what the run determines.

planning.outcome: One receipted estimate at the preregistered beyond-reach target, with variance and effective sample size, or a recorded unusable outcome
